confirmed: The complete markdown conversion was read through its final references; the PDF has 21 pages and its first-page margin identifies arXiv:2409.05747v1 [cs.HC], 9 Sep 2024. The form correctly identifies the version read rather than treating it as the 2025 journal article (PDF p. 1 and document page count).
The title and authors are A Novel Idea Generation Tool using a Structured Conversational AI (CAI) System, B. Sankar and Dibakar Sen (PDF p. 1).

Randomization concerns division into six groups and assignment of design problems. The protocol describes conventional ideation in Part A and CAI-assisted ideation in Part B for each designer; it reports no randomized AI allocation or randomized condition order. The quasi_people design and observational context classifications are supported (PDF pp. 8-10, Sections 6, 6.1.3 and 6.1.4).

Thirty postgraduate product design students were recruited, with five designers per group. A separate analyzed-person count and exclusions are not reported, so the form's null analyzed counts are defensible; the designer sample is below 50, regardless of the larger rater counts (PDF p. 8, Section 6; p. 9, Section 6.1.3).
Both parts were allocated 20 minutes. Part A prohibited computers and other digital gadgets; Part B involved use of the CAI tool and shortlisting potential ideas (PDF p. 9, Section 6.1.3).

Part A involved idea generation by each designer, whereas Part B involved collective refinement and curation of GPT ideas as a group. The AI condition therefore includes human assistance and curation, supporting observational context rather than a purely AI-versus-human-output design (PDF p. 10, Section 6.1.4 continuation).

The fluency reported string is exact: conventional versus CAI-aided ideation produced averages of 4.8 and 15 ideas in 20 minutes. Figure 6 displays the six problem statements; these are group/problem outputs, not six people or 30 independent participant scores (PDF p. 10, Section 6.2.2; p. 12, Figure 6).

The novelty reported string is exact: Part A 2.5 and Part B 3.86. The text specifies individual-idea ratings on a 1 to 5 Likert scale by 80 experts; these are the prose-reported means, not values recalculated from the chart (PDF p. 10, Section 6.2.2; p. 12, Figures 7-8).

The variety reported string is exact: Part A 2.9 and Part B 4.2. The method describes sets of twelve ideas sampled from about 80 ideas, rated by 80 experts on a 1 to 5 scale. These idea and rater counts do not count toward the participant threshold (PDF p. 10, Section 6.2.3; p. 12, continuation and Figure 9).

The one-line finding reproduces all three reported mean comparisons correctly. No inferential test statistics, standard errors, confidence intervals, or standardized effects for these comparisons are printed in the results (PDF pp. 10-13, Sections 6.2-6.3 and Figures 5-10).

The twenty experts judging meaningfulness and the 80 experts judging novelty/variety are evaluators, not the sample receiving the ideation intervention; the paper does not establish whether these evaluator groups overlap (PDF p. 10, Sections 6.1.5 and 6.2.1-6.2.3).

The later structured-prompt comparison illustrates proposed changes; the authors explicitly say expert assessment of that approach is still pending. It supplies no additional randomized people study (PDF pp. 17-18, Section 7.4 and Figure 15; p. 18, Section 8).

This is an original tool-development and pilot-study paper, not a synthesis, so the default synthesis fields are appropriate. No appendix or separately identified supplement appears in the complete document (PDF pp. 1-21).
summary: The 30-student pilot does not report randomized AI assistance and remains observational context. The reported means and source version are correct, but GPT-4 identification, participant country, and two omitted outcomes need correction.
